messages.subject: Number of occasions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I'm working with photographic records from camera trapping, the monitoring was carried out from November 22, 2014 to September 22, 2016. My question is, for this case it's necessary to work with different sessions? Because with just one session, there are 121 occasions and I don't know if it's appropriate to work with this number of occasions.

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: Number of occasions
messages.body_plain:
The target species is the black bear (Ursus americanus) and it's the first time that population density is calculated in this area. The cameras were moving during the two years. I used the package camtrapR to define the duration of the occasions and based on this, each occasion lasts 7 days.

About using open secr, I was thinking which is better in this case because I'm working with records from another place, but this monitoring lasted only 2 months and I used closed secr to calculate the density.

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: Number of occasions
messages.body_plain:
Do you have any hypotheses for defining sessions?
bear behaviour: mating vs non mating
calendar: winter vs summer
resources: different time of the year with different food resources.
design: consistency in camera trap array

The choice of a session should follow a research question and not the opposite. What I mean here is that when you create your multisession you will calculate different densities for each session. If you don't have a clear hypothesis to define these sessions, then it is going to be difficult to discuss an observed change, or absence of change in density.

If you want to compare with the second site, you could do that separately by subsampling your long monitoring to match the 2 months monitoring from the second site.
Then you can use a multisession model with each site being a session.

Seb

messages.subject: Re: Number of occasions
messages.body_plain:
The main objective of doing this is to calculate density for 5 sites for the first time, I didn't think of a hypothesis to define the sessions because I just wanted to get an estimate of the density. I thought, at some point, to compare the density between sites and also compare between years within each site but I don't know if this can help me to define the sessions.

One of the important events that changes the behavior of the bear is hibernation, although in Mexico it's different from the bears that live in USA or Canada because they don't hibernate all winter, enter and leave the den several times or do not hibernate (mostly males). Spring is a period of resources shortage (relative) but summer and fall are important seasons for black bear because they increase food consumption to prepare for winter, this is called hyperphagia.

messages.subject: Re: Number of occasions
messages.body_plain:
So it seems that you have two main questions here.
difference between 5 sites
seasonal change within one site
Some ideas:
For the first question, you could fit a multisession model with one session per site (5 sessions) => one estimate of density per site
Each session can have a different number of occasions, but the general monitoring effort should be kept as similar as possible.
If one site has only two months of monitoring, maybe you should try to keep a similar duration and seasonality for the other sites.
You could also fit multiple sessions of 2 months or longer sessions in the longer sites to test for variations which could help understand the information available for the sites with only one session of two months.

I am not sure how much change in density you expect to observe from one year to the following one.
It seems to me that for the second question you are more looking at seasonal activity than seasonal density.
This can also be done with your camera trap data but the analysis is different.

I hope that helps a little bit

messages.subject: Relationship between covariates and D estimate
messages.subject_clean: Relationship between covariates and D estimate
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to model the relationship between D estimate and three spatial covariates (elevation, NDVI, and ruggedness) in a multi-session SECR model. The model runs properly and the predicted D surface also looks reasonable. I am now interested in visualising the relationship between each of the variables and D. I am using the predict function for this, but I need to mention values for all the three covariates in the newdata argument for the code to work.

If I am interested in the relationship between D and NDVI only, could I keep the elevation constant and ruggedness constant to interpret the relationship. Here is the code that I am using. Is there a better method of interpreting this relationship?

#Model:
multi.full1<-secr.fit(msSL1, model=list(D~elev+I(elev^2)+ndvi+I(ndvi^2)+rug, sigma~1),mask=covmask.list,details =list(autoini =10),trace =FALSE,detectfn="HHN", optim(method="Nelder-Mead"))

#relationship with NDVI and D, keeping elevation and ruggedness constant
temp<-predict(multi.full, newdata=data.frame(ndvi=seq(-0.5,1,0.01), elev=rep(0.1,151), rug=rep(0.1,151)))

I tried min and max values of elevation, but the relationship with NDVI and D is similar, only it scales with elevation.

Many thanks,
Manvi

messages.subject: Spatial-Mark Resight - SEs of 0 & Inability to model sex
messages.subject_clean: Spatial-Mark Resight - SEs of 0 & Inability to model sex
messages.body_plain:
Hi secr group! I hope this finds all well.

I am writing as I have ran into two issues. I apologise in advance if it’s something obvious – it’s my first time using mark-resight models! I have looked through this forum as well as others, but to no avail.

I am implementing sightings-only SMR models in secr 4.1, to estimate density of a lion population from camera trap data. I applied standard SECR models to this data with success, by identifying animals through individual markings. However, given that about 25% of the detections could not be IDd, I decided to try and apply mark-resight models.

As there was no way to know for sure whether unresolved detections were of marked but unidentifiable or of unmarked individuals, all unresolved detections were initially classified as marked but unidentifiable. This was to avoid misidentifying a marked individual as an unmarked individual and introducing a positive bias (as per Rich et al. 2019’s paper, also on lions). This left me with a Tm file (and no Tu or Tn file).

First Issue - SEs of 0

My first issue is that, while the estimated densities are realistic, my SEs and CIs are of 0 – as so:

Fitted (real) parameters evaluated at base levels of covariates

       link     estimate  SE.estimate          lcl          ucl

D       log 2.534081e-04 0.000000e+00 2.534081e-04 2.534081e-04

g0    logit 5.953364e-03 1.258175e-03 3.932561e-03 9.003200e-03

sigma   log 4.793594e+03 5.193539e+02 3.878897e+03 5.923991e+03

Has anyone had a similar issue before?

Interestingly, when I read the Tm file as a Tu file instead (so assuming all unidentified were actually unmarked), I obtained very similar density estimates as when it was read in as the Tm file, and realistic SEs and CIs (so ‘fixing’ the problem, if you will). However, for the reasons explained above I do not think this is what I should be doing for this specific dataset.

Similarly, if I read the Tm file + a Tu file with a few randomly-placed 0s – even with only one  single zero, actually – it behaves fine. If, I do the same but the Tu is all 0s, on the other hand, I go back to getting SEs of 0.

Second issue - Inability to model effect of sex

In addition, none of the SMR work when trying to model sex as a covariate (giving NAs for both D and SE). I saw that the manual mentions that finite mixtures are only “partially implemented” – does anyone know whether this is likely to be the reason, or if it is indeed possible to model the effect of sex on sigma and g0, and my issue stems from something else?

Any help would be massively appreciated – I’ve been trying to figure this out for a while and there’s nothing more I can think of trying!

Thanks so much in advance for anyone who could provide any input. I’ve attached the input files, as I’ve seen others do so on this forum (except the 'dummy' Tu file mentioned above, as it was simply the same as Tm but with all 0s interspersed with a few random 1s). Please do let me know if there’s anything which is unclear or which I did not explain well.

Thanks and all the best,

Paolo

messages.subject_clean: Spatial-Mark Resight - SEs of 0 & Inability to model sex
messages.body_plain:
I'm sure Murray can help with fitting issues, but I had some general comments.

What is the goal of including the unidentified photos--to deal with unmarked individuals or to try to increase precision by using more data? The main idea of mark resight is that one subset of individuals is marked and another is unmarked. The unmarked individuals must be considered because they have a capture probability of 0 if you require their individual identity and thus introduce extreme individual heterogeneity in capture probability and negative bias in N and D. If you cannot tell if any observations are in fact unmarked, a spatial mark resight will not solve this problem of individual heterogeneity in detection. If all unknown ID observations are classified as "marked but not identifiable", the density of the unmarked portion of the population will be estimated very close to 0. This may be related to the estimation problems you are seeing, but probably doesn't explain them all.Further, you should not pool observations of potentially unmarked individuals with marked individuals in the "marked but not identifiable" class. The correct class is "unknown marked status", though I don't believe secr handles that class. But without any unmarked observations, reclassifying these observations will not solve the problem.

Regarding precision: if you must classify all unknown ID photos as "marked but not identifiable", all data are of the same class of individual--marked. Therefore, a more appropriate model would be one with only 1 class of individual--a "random thinning" model. This has been developed, but not published to my knowledge. The reason it has not been published is that the unknown ID observations only increase precision in sampling scenarios with almost no identified photos.

Given these points, I believe you should stick with regular SCR and accept you might underestimate density if there are indeed some unmarked individuals in the population.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Number of occasions
messages.body_plain:
Good day,

Where chimpanzees were camera trapped for ten months, we included a maximum of 1 obs / individual / day, so we could have had a very large number of daily occasions. Instead, we grouped the data into weekly occasions, where the detector type was "count proximity", and individuals could be detected up to 7 times per occasion (binomial distribution of size 7 for the counts). This allowed us to model differences in detectability between seasons. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/ajp.22647

I think that if you're not going to model temporal variation, you could use the count detector type and have no discrete temporal occasions. Here's a link to Murray's paper describing SECR methods without discrete temporal occasions https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/08-1735.1

Sessions could then be used to group animals or sets of detectors instead of temporal subsets of the data.

All the best,
Eric

messages.subject: Missing areas
messages.body_plain:
Hello group,

I am working with several communities that are collaborating to monitor an endangered grizzly population. The overall density is approximately 2.8 bears/1000km2. From previous research, I know that the approximate female and male sigma is 3.91km and 11.48 km respectively and that the population is small and isolated.

The current project is ongoing and they are planning to sample every second year. After their first year, in 2019, it seems as though the sampling is somewhat uneven (see image below), and there are a few "holes" and areas with lower sampling intensity. They did 4 occasions at each site in 2019 and plan to repeat in 2021.

On Wednesday, February 19, 2020 at 4:07:16 PM UTC, baugusti wrote:

> I'm sure Murray can help with fitting issues, but I had some general comments.
>
> What is the goal of including the unidentified photos--to deal with unmarked individuals or to try to increase precision by using more data? The main idea of mark resight is that one subset of individuals is marked and another is unmarked. The unmarked individuals must be considered because they have a capture probability of 0 if you require their individual identity and thus introduce extreme individual heterogeneity in capture probability and negative bias in N and D. If you cannot tell if any observations are in fact unmarked, a spatial mark resight will not solve this problem of individual heterogeneity in detection. If all unknown ID observations are classified as "marked but not identifiable", the density of the unmarked portion of the population will be estimated very close to 0. This may be related to the estimation problems you are seeing, but probably doesn't explain them all.Further, you should not pool observations of potentially unmarked individuals with marked individuals in the "marked but not identifiable" class. The correct class is "unknown marked status", though I don't believe secr handles that class. But without any unmarked observations, reclassifying these observations will not solve the problem.
>
> Regarding precision: if you must classify all unknown ID photos as "marked but not identifiable", all data are of the same class of individual--marked. Therefore, a more appropriate model would be one with only 1 class of individual--a "random thinning" model. This has been developed, but not published to my knowledge. The reason it has not been published is that the unknown ID observations only increase precision in sampling scenarios with almost no identified photos.
>
> Given these points, I believe you should stick with regular SCR and accept you might underestimate density if there are indeed some unmarked individuals in the population.
>
> Ben
>
>
>
>
>
>

I applied standard SECR models to this data with success, by identifying animals through individual markings. However, given that about 25% of the detections could not be IDd, I decided to try and apply mark-resight models.
> >
> > As there was no way to know for sure whether unresolved detections were of marked but unidentifiable or of unmarked individuals, all unresolved detections were initially classified as marked but unidentifiable. This was to avoid misidentifying a marked individual as an unmarked individual and introducing a positive bias (as per Rich et al. 2019’s paper, also on lions). This left me with a Tm file (and no Tu or Tn file).
> >
> >
> > First Issue - SEs of 0

However, for the reasons explained above I do not think this is what I should be doing for this specific dataset.

messages.subject: secr 4.2.0
messages.body_plain:
The main change in this version concerns the number of threads used when fitting models. This now defaults to 2 rather than one less than the maximum.  Set the 'ncores' argument of secr.fit() or setNumThreads() for more. The change was needed for compliance with CRAN policy; with the new default a single user is less likely to hog resources on a multi-user system.

A new random systematic design 'lacework' is introduced e.g., make.lacework(). fxi.secr() and related functions are enabled for polygon detector types.
